rich_summary: This episode recounts the event that sets in motion King Parikshit’s fatal curse. While hunting in the forest, the Kuru king wounds a deer and pursues it until he becomes exhausted and thirsty. He encounters the sage Samika (unnamed here but implied) sitting silently in meditation and asks about the deer. Because the sage is observing a vow of silence, he does not respond. Irritated and fatigued, Parikshit places a dead snake on the sage’s shoulders as an insult, but soon regrets his act and departs. The sage himself forgives the king, recognizing it as a mistake. However, the sage’s fiery young son Sringin hears of the insult from another boy and, inflamed with anger and pride in his ascetic power, curses Parikshit to die within seven days from the bite of the serpent king Takshaka. The moment illustrates the dangers of anger, the power of ascetic speech, and the fragile relationship between kings and sages.

highlight_spans.why: Introduces King Parikshit, situating him in the Kuru lineage and setting up the royal figure whose small mistake will have enormous consequences.
The pivotal insult: Parikshit places a dead snake on the silent sage’s shoulder, the action that triggers the entire chain of events.
Description of Sringin, the sage’s powerful and temperamental son, foreshadowing the destructive potential of his anger.
Sringin’s furious reaction on hearing of the insult to his father, marking the emotional turning point before the curse.
The formal curse declaring that Takshaka will kill Parikshit within seven nights—one of the most consequential pronouncements in the narrative.

top_scenes.scene_text: The exhausted King Parikshit in a forest clearing lifting a dead snake with the tip of his bow and placing it across the silent sage’s shoulders as the ascetic sits motionless in meditation.
Young Sringin, eyes blazing with anger beside a forest stream, touching water in ritual as he pronounces the deadly curse against King Parikshit.
The tranquil sage seated in a cow-pen surrounded by calves and cows, unknowingly bearing the dead snake across his shoulders while remaining absorbed in silence.
